chapter: Los Angeles nightlife: Sheffield, Hamp and the Cotton Club
title: Officer Sheffield, the tough Prohibition detective
summary: Joe describes Sheffield as a huge Black detective who raided bootleg joints but spared musicians, and the Sonny Clay record named for him.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Do you know Officer Sheffield?
Oh, do I remember Sheffield!
Tell me a little about him.
Anybody that knew anything about Prohibition remembers Sheffield. He was a tough cop, man. Sheffield would arrest his mother if she's bootlegging.
Darensbourg - 173
Was he a big guy, a small guy or what?

He liked musicians. He was a great big guy, big as Joe Louis, or bigger -- or Larry Holmes, the heavyweight champion. And about just as strong, too, because I seen him pitch guys out of windows and everything. But he never bothered musicians.
Well, the reason that I asked you is because he seems to be a local character around here...
He was that.
At least among the old-time Los Angeles musicians.
I'm trying to think of his partner. I think Sheffield's partner was named Benny.
He was a regular beat patrolman or what?
No, no, he was a detective. And you would be in a place, in a bootlegging joint, and they'd have guys watching out, and then you'd hear that son...then here comes Sheffield! [LAUGHS]
What was his first name? Do you remember his first name?
I think his name was Roy.
I don't know if you knew this, but I think it was Shirley Clay's band or somebody that recorded...
Sonny Clay?
Darensbourg - 174
I mean Sonny Clay. They recorded a thing called "Sheffield Blues." And everybody was trying to think, "Where is this Sheffield? Was it named after the town of Sheffield somewhere, or..."
No, it must have been named after Officer Sheffield.
Because Blakeney is playing trumpet on that, too; that's Blakeney's first record. So he must have been a local character.
